title: Boss: the settlement service hangs every Friday
summary: A three-way transfer cycle, two semaphores taken in opposite orders by async code, and a wait-for graph tool that finds the cycle in a dump.

steps.title: The ticket
body: **INC-6033: settlement stops on Fridays at 17:00 (batch + live traffic). Restart fixes it.**
Index         SyncBlock MonitorHeld Recursion Owning Thread Info          SyncBlock Owner
Three threads in `Transfer`, each owning one account lock and waiting for another: a three-way cycle. And, separately, async code
stuck on two semaphores. Fix both, then build the little tool that would have found the cycle for you.

steps.title: 1. A cycle of three
prompt: The Friday batch moves money around a ring of accounts: `a` to `b`, `b` to `c`, `c` to `a`, all at once. Fix
**`Ledger.Transfer(Account from, Account to, int amount)`** so no combination of transfers can deadlock. `Account` has an `Id` and a
**Checked:** three threads, one per transfer of 10, under every interleaving (or every one with up to two preemptions, which is
enough to build a three-way cycle). Balances must end at `100 100 100`.
starter: public static void Transfer(Account from, Account to, int amount)
solution: public static void Transfer(Account from, Account to, int amount)
var (first, second) = from.Id < to.Id ? (from, to) : (to, from);

interleavings.title: a to b, b to c, c to a

hints: A cycle needs someone to take a higher lock before a lower one. A total order on all accounts rules that out.
Order the two accounts by `Id` and always lock the smaller id first.

steps.title: 2. Two semaphores, two orders
prompt: `Payouts` protects the payout table with `_payouts` and the ledger with `_ledger` (both `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)`). `ApproveAsync`
takes `_payouts` then `_ledger`; `RefundAsync` takes `_ledger` then `_payouts`. Under load they wait for each other forever.
Fix **`Payouts`** so that `ApproveAsync(string id, Func<Task> work)` and `RefundAsync(string id, Func<Task> work)` both still hold
**both** semaphores while they run `work`, can run at the same time without hanging, and always release what they took.
starter: public async Task ApproveAsync(string id, Func<Task> work)
public async Task RefundAsync(string id, Func<Task> work)
solution: public Task ApproveAsync(string id, Func<Task> work) => WithBothAsync(work);
public Task RefundAsync(string id, Func<Task> work) => WithBothAsync(work);
// Every caller takes the two gates in the same order: payouts, then ledger.
template: var dojoCalls = Enumerable.Range(0, 20).Select(i => i % 2 == 0 ? dojoP.ApproveAsync($"p{i}", DojoWork) : dojoP.RefundAsync($"r{i}", DojoWork)).ToArray();
var dojoDone = await Task.WhenAny(dojoAll, Task.Delay(4000)) == dojoAll;
Dojo.Check("Approvals and refunds running together all finish", dojoDone, "They were still waiting after 4 seconds: the two semaphores are taken in opposite orders.");
Dojo.Eq("Work never overlaps (both gates are held while it runs)", 1, dojoMax);
Dojo.Check("Both gates are free afterwards", await Task.WhenAny(dojoAfter, Task.Delay(2000)) == dojoAfter, "A gate was never released.");
hints: Lock ordering applies to semaphores too. Make both methods take `_payouts` first, then `_ledger`.
Simplest: one private `WithBothAsync(Func<Task> work)` that takes the two gates in a fixed order, used by both public methods.

steps.title: 3. Find the cycle
prompt: From `syncblk` and `clrstack` you can build a **wait-for graph**: for each blocked thread, the thread that owns the lock it waits for.
A deadlock is a cycle in that graph. Write the tool.
**`static List<int>? FindCycle(IReadOnlyDictionary<int, int> waitsFor)`**: `waitsFor[t] = u` means thread `t` waits for a lock owned
by thread `u` (each thread waits for at most one). Return the threads of a cycle, **starting at its smallest thread id** and in wait
order, or `null` if there is none. If there are several cycles, return the one containing the smallest thread id that is in any
Example: `{21: 22, 22: 23, 23: 21, 30: 21}` gives `[21, 22, 23]` (30 waits on the cycle but is not part of it).
solution: if (!waitsFor.TryGetValue(t, out var next)) { t = -1; break; }
if (best is null || cycle[0] < best[0]) best = cycle;
template: Dojo.Eq("The three-way cycle from the dump", new List<int> { 21, 22, 23 }, FindCycle(new Dictionary<int, int> { [21] = 22, [22] = 23, [23] = 21, [30] = 21 }));
Dojo.Eq("It starts at the smallest id", new List<int> { 12, 17 }, FindCycle(new Dictionary<int, int> { [17] = 12, [12] = 17 }));
Dojo.Check("A chain of waits without a cycle is not a deadlock", FindCycle(new Dictionary<int, int> { [1] = 2, [2] = 3, [4] = 3 }) is null, "There is no cycle here: return null.");
Dojo.Check("No waits, no deadlock", FindCycle(new Dictionary<int, int>()) is null, "Return null for an empty graph.");
Dojo.Eq("Two cycles: the one with the smallest id", new List<int> { 3, 9 }, FindCycle(new Dictionary<int, int> { [8] = 5, [5] = 8, [9] = 3, [3] = 9, [40] = 9 }));
Dojo.Eq("A thread waiting for itself (a non-reentrant lock)", new List<int> { 7 }, FindCycle(new Dictionary<int, int> { [7] = 7 }));
hints: From each thread, follow `waitsFor` until you reach a thread with no entry (no cycle) or a thread you already visited on this walk (a cycle starts there).

Keep the walk in a list with each thread's position; the cycle is the part of the list from the repeated thread on. Rotate it so the smallest id comes first, and keep the cycle with the smallest first id.
explain: This is how database engines find deadlocks (SQL Server's lock monitor and PostgreSQL's `deadlock_timeout` check walk a wait-for
graph) and then pick a victim to abort. The .NET runtime does not do this for `lock`: a Monitor deadlock waits forever, which is
why lock-wait timeouts and dumps matter.
